summary.en: Katie makes the case that beauty and functionality are not opposites - beautiful design actually improves usability, trust, and approachability. She traces how the word "beauty" faded from digitized books as functionality became king, and why that mindset is mistaken. The episode shows how investing in craft pays off in user trust and business results.
summary.zh: 凯蒂指出，美与功能并非对立——美观的设计实际上能提升可用性、信任感与亲和力。她追溯了随着"功能为王"观念的盛行，"美"一词如何从数字化书籍中消退，并说明这种想法是错误的。本期展示了在设计工艺上的投入如何转化为用户信任与商业成果。

turns.speaker: Katie Dill
turns.en: The use of the word beauty in books that have been digitized by Google has decreased, like pretty dramatically. And it's aligned with this idea of, "Well, functionality is king. Functionality is what matters." As if people think about functionality and beauty as like two opposite things. No, they're not two opposite things. Functionality is important. And actually beauty enhances functionality because it does make things easier to use, more approachable, more compelling to use. (00:00:32): And the other piece of it that is not talked about in business as often is just the importance of how people feel. Things that are more beautiful, increase trust. You see that we've put painstaking detail into this, and we care about the details of how something works, and that gives you assurance that we care about other details that you can't see too.
turns.zh:
谷歌数字化书籍中“美”这个词的使用频率大幅下降。这与一种观点不谋而合，即“功能至上”。人们似乎把功能性和美观视为截然相反的两个概念。但实际上，两者并非对立面。功能性固然重要，而美观恰恰能提升功能性——它让产品更易用、更亲切、更引人入胜。（00:00:32）  
还有一点在商业语境中常被忽视，那就是用户体验的重要性。美观的设计能增强信任感。当人们看到产品精心打磨的细节时，会感受到我们对功能性同样用心，这会让用户相信，我们在处理那些看不见的细节时同样用心。

turns.speaker: Katie Dill
turns.en: Yeah. No, I'm happy to talk about it because, frankly, it was the biggest learning experience of my leadership career, or at least that happened in one moment. It happened in my early days at Airbnb. I was hired to take on the Design Organization, or the Experience Design Organization. That's basically the Product Design team, which was 10 people at the time. They had been reporting directly to one of the founders and they were going to start reporting to me. (00:05:47): During my interview process I learned a lot about what was working, and what wasn't working, and some of the trials and tribulations with the Design Organization and its collaboration with others. So it seemed like there was room for improvement in how Engineering, and Product Management, and Design all worked together. There was also really low engagement scores in the Design team. (00:06:08): So I kind of came in ready to go and excited to try to help make some change based on all the things that I had learned from various leaders and people across the company. I came in swinging, ready to go. And then about a month into my time there, I got a meeting on my calendar, Thursday 8:30 AM, it was an hour and a half with half of the Design team, so that was five people, and our HR partner.
turns.zh: 是的。不，我很乐意谈论这件事，因为坦白说，这是我领导生涯中最宝贵的学习经历，或者至少是在那一刻发生的。这件事发生在我加入Airbnb的早期阶段。我被聘来接管设计部门，也就是体验设计团队。当时这个团队有10个人，他们一直直接向公司创始人汇报，现在要改为向我汇报。（00:05:47）在面试过程中，我了解到很多关于设计部门运作成效不佳的地方，以及与其他部门合作时遇到的挑战。因此，工程、产品管理和设计团队之间的协作似乎存在改进空间。同时，设计团队的敬业度评分也非常低。（00:06:08）所以我满怀信心地加入了这家公司，准备根据从公司各级领导和同事那里学到的东西推动变革。我一上任就积极投入，准备大展身手。然而，在我到职一个月后，日程表上安排了一场会议，时间是周四上午8:30，参加者包括设计团队的一半成员，即5个人，以及我们的人力资源伙伴。

turns.speaker: Lenny

turns.speaker: Katie Dill
turns.en: Yeah. And I remember this so vividly. I remember walking into the office, and all the rooms in Airbnb's office are very unique spaces that look like Airbnb's. But of course this was the one room with all white walls and just a gray flat rectangle table. I walked into the room and there were five of them seated around the table. They had a pack of papers in front of them and they went on taking turns quietly reading from the papers all the things that they saw that I was doing wrong and all the things that they didn't like about me. (00:07:22): It was a really hard moment there. I went through all the usual kind of like stages of grief when one hears feedback, which is just like an immediate want to respond to be like, "Yeah." Like, "Well there was a good reason for that." And like, "That's not how it actually was." And, "This is why I did that." But luckily, thank goodness I had the sense to just listen and not respond in that way. I mean, clearly what they were telling me is that that was one of the things that was missing. (00:07:49): So I heard them out and took it all in. And regardless of each individual saying, what was very clear was that the missing piece, the theme that was across all of that, is that I hadn't earned their trust. So whether how right or how wrong what I was doing was, is the key piece is that I wasn't bringing the team along with me. They had no idea that they could trust in what I was trying to build, and what I was trying to shape, and that I cared about them, and that I had their best interests and shared goals at heart. And that was absolutely my fault. (00:08:24): In retrospect, as hard as that was, I'm very grateful and very amazed that they could come together and share that with me. It can be hard to bring feedback forward like that. So it was an extremely valuable learning experience. I took from that to then immediately shift how I was operating. And really a key part in building trust was to listen, to hear out what the individuals on the team were setting out to do, what they cared about, what motivated them. (00:08:57): So I started to make pretty fast change and still moving in the direction that was necessary for the org to make the really large impact in how we were operating, but bringing folks along with me. You can inflict change on people, but if you want to do it with them trust is the key element there. And then a couple months later, we had the best engagement scores in the company. (00:09:20): So it did objectively improve the situation, and since then taken that on into next steps in other companies that I've joined. And just think about instead of coming in swinging, come in listening, so that you can really set out to make change that actually has true, positive impact on the folks around you and that you bring along with you.
turns.zh: 是啊。我记得这件事特别清楚。我记得走进Airbnb办公室时，那里的每个房间都独具特色，充满Airbnb的风格。但当然，那间房间是唯一墙壁全白、只有一张灰色矩形桌子的房间。我走进房间时，看到五个人围坐在桌旁。他们面前放着一堆文件，轮流默默地从文件中读出我做错的所有事情，以及他们不喜欢我的地方。（00:07:22）：那真是一个艰难的时刻。当听到反馈时，我经历了常见的悲伤阶段——比如，第一反应就是想反驳：“不，这么做肯定有充分理由。”“事实并非如此。”“我当时是出于这样的考虑。”但幸运的是，我还算明智，选择了倾听而非反驳。显然，他们想告诉我，这就是缺失的关键环节。（00:07:49）：所以我听完了他们的话，认真领会了每个人的发言。无论每个人具体说了什么，有一点非常明确，那就是缺失的部分、贯穿所有反馈的主题，就是我没有赢得他们的信任。无论我做得对与否，关键在于我没有让团队与我同行。他们不知道可以信任我正在努力打造的东西，信任我的决策，信任我关心他们，信任我怀揣共同目标。这完全是我的过错。（00:08:24）：回想起来，尽管那时很痛苦，但我非常感激也惊讶于他们能坦诚地分享这些反馈。能这样直白地提出反馈并不容易。这是一次极其宝贵的学习经历。基于此，我立即调整了自己的管理方式。建立信任的关键在于倾听，倾听团队成员的目标、关切和动机。（00:08:57）：所以我很快做出了改变，继续朝着让团队参与进来、共同达成目标的方向前进。你可以强制推行变革，但若想获得信任，关键在于让团队参与其中。几个月后，我们的员工敬业度评分创下公司新高。

（00:10:21）不过，你提到的Thayer项目实际上是我非常重视的举措。每周多次召集设计团队在关键时刻集合，共同构建设计社区。正如Airbnb的Joebot曾说：“比如，你穿哪件T恤？你属于哪个团队？” 我回应道：“你有两件T恤，一件是设计团队专属，另一件是市场团队专属，或者你参与的跨学科团队专属。因为这两个团队都非常重要，但构建社区的侧重点略有不同。” 所以，Thayer项目为此提供了绝佳平台。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Zooming out a little bit, I think the elephant in the room a lot of times with design is this idea that I'd say most PMs, most founders, intellectually understand the value of design, understand the value of high quality. But day-to-day it's often not actually prioritized versus new features, new product launches, partly because the ROI is just really unclear. (00:11:16): If we spend another month making this more awesome and making this even more amazing design-wise, experience-wise, what is that going to get us? Clearly, at Airbnb design was highly prioritized. At Stripe, from an outsider's perspective, it clearly is. I'm just curious what you've learned about how to make the case for the ROI of design and just how Stripe, and Airbnb, and Lyft have done that.
turns.zh: 退一步看，我认为设计领域常被忽视的一个关键问题是，大多数产品经理和创始人虽然在理性层面认可设计的价值，理解高质量设计的重要性，但在日常工作中却往往将其置于次要地位，优先处理新功能开发和产品发布，部分原因在于设计的ROI（投资回报率）难以量化。（00:11:16）比如，如果我们再花一个月时间优化设计、提升用户体验，这能带来什么实际收益？显然，Airbnb高度重视设计。从外部视角看，Stripe也显然如此。我很好奇你们是如何论证设计的ROI的，以及Stripe、Airbnb和Lyft是如何做到这一点的。

turns.speaker: Katie Dill
turns.en: It's a great question, and I think this is like an age-old question that I don't know if will ever go away, and probably because the quality bar keeps evolving, keeps rising. But I think first to kind of level set before we dive into that I would say that there are levels of quality. There is the, does the thing work? Does it provide some sort of value proposition? It like executes on its job. That's baseline quality. (00:12:06): Next is that, does it do it exceedingly well? Is it error-free? Actually, maybe that's not even exceedingly well but just error-free and it actually works in a well-rounded way. Then beyond that, like level three, level four, level five, does it exceed expectations and it does something that you weren't even seeking for as a user? And I do think the levels of quality should be based on user expectations. I don't believe that there are disciplines that just don't care about quality. (00:12:36): I think it's more about that prioritization and kind of like what you talked about is just like, is it really worth getting something to that exceedingly well state or is it, what about just like another feature and being seduced by the chase of another feature versus actually taking your features to a level of being great? That is hard. And I get it when you look at your user base and they're all shouting from the rooftops for this additional feature. (00:13:05): Of course you're going to want to prioritize that over something they never asked for. Then the other thing would be you end up with like you've got three things that you could possibly do to make perhaps the next stage in your product development. Two of them you know you can measure and they're going to line up to business goals, and one of them you can't. 这是个很棒的问题。我觉得这是一个古老的难题，不知道是否会永远存在，或许正是因为质量标准在不断提升。但在深入探讨之前，我想先厘清一个概念：质量有不同的层次。首先是"东西能不能正常运行"，能否提供某种价值主张？能否胜任本职工作？这就是基础质量。（00:12:06）接下来是"能否做到极致出色"？有没有零缺陷？即便不追求极致，至少也要确保无故障、功能完备。再往上层次，三、四、五级质量，要求超越用户预期，甚至提供超出预期的功能。这里的标准应该基于用户的期望。我不相信有不重视质量的行业。（00:12:36）关键在于优先级排序。比如，当用户疯狂呼吁某个新功能时，你会不会倾向于先做这个，而忽视真正需要提升的功能？这很难抉择。当你观察用户群体时，他们往往对某个新功能趋之若鹜，却忽视了真正能提升用户体验的功能。（00:13:05）当然，面对用户迫切需求的功能，你会优先处理。但另一种情况是，你有三个可选方案来推进产品开发，其中两个可量化且符合商业目标，第三个则难以评估。（00:13:21）显然，人们更容易追逐可量化的目标，但那些深知质量是不可妥协的长期核心要素的公司，不会陷入数字游戏。他们明白，功能固然重要，但真正决定产品易用性和吸引力的关键在于这些功能的质量。（00:13:53）这就像健身的例子。我不知道你怎么想，但每次想锻炼时，脑子里总有个声音问：“今天真的要去吗？一天的锻炼能让我拥有六块腹肌吗？”当然不可能。但随后我会意识到：“如果今天不去，再拖一天又怎样？” （00:14:21）归根结底，坚持这些理念最终会带来更好的结果，如同健康长寿的人生。因此，我希望能坚持锻炼。我相信全球一些顶尖公司也秉持同样的理念。虽然用户未必主动提出需求，但比如在客服案例中就能发现端倪——用户显然不清楚如何使用新功能，这很可能是质量问题，或者他们正期待更完善的功能。（00:14:53）有些二、三、四级质量标准，可能用户不会主动要求。但我再举个例子：如果没有竞争对手，那当然无所谓。想想第一辆车吧，我敢肯定车轮转动很费力，
那个座位肯定不舒服，而且只要是黑色，你想选什么颜色都可以。对吧？但当时没有竞争对手。竞争对手是一匹马，所以没关系。如今对汽车而言，关键在于缝线、皮革材质选择以及车门的声音。（00:15:28）这些细节决定了一辆普通车和高价值豪华车的区别。关键在于理解细节的重要性，以及如何通过卓越的执行力将品质提升到新高度。最后，要说的是，我知道有种说法是增长与质量二选一，但实际上质量就是增长。如果你能让产品更易用、更易懂，用户自然会更愿意使用它、更多地使用它，并获得更好的体验，进而主动向他人推荐。（00:16:08）在Stripe，我们的增长团队可以说痴迷于打造卓越的用户体验，因为我们亲眼见证了这与业务指标的直接关联。比如，我们改进了注册流程，让产品更易懂，帮助用户理解不同场景下的使用方式，最终激活量因这些质量改进而显著提升。（00:16:38）我见过的最能体现质量对业务影响的例子之一，是在结账体验方面。我们研究了多家顶级电商网站的结账流程，发现99%的头部电商存在功能缺陷，严重阻碍了流畅、快速的结账流程，进而影响转化率。这些细节本质上是质量问题。（00:17:14）关键在于，你若真正理解用户的使用需求，就能优化体验。多年来，我们一直专注于此，致力于为商家和消费者打造更优的结账体验。通过对大大小小的细节进行优化，我们成功将旧版结账流程的收入提升了10.5%至新版结账流程的水平。这些微妙的改进对提升营收效果显著。

turns.zh: 老实说，我对这种把事情分成“商业目标”和“设计目标”的说法很反感。因为我觉得，首先我们应该讨论的是：“我们到底要打造什么？” 我认为，那些想创造真正有影响力产品的团队，应该致力于打造高质量的产品，真正为客户提供积极有益的服务，因为他们深知这才是长远发展商业的关键。（00:19:47）：所以没错，在这个过程中，可能存在轻微的优先级差异。比如设计师可能更关注情感体验和用户感受，因为这正是他们的思维方式，而这也是一个重要的视角。另一些人则会说：“那就把按钮做大点，用户点击率自然就高了，这才是我们想要的结果。” （00:20:10）：这就是为什么我强调多学科团队密切协作的重要性，因为有时候我们就是对话中的制衡力量。但关键是，如果我们能达成共识：我们要打造什么样的产品？我们要打造伟大的产品吗？那么我们就能认识到，实用性固然重要，但可用性和吸引力同样不可或缺，因为这些因素共同构成了伟大的产品。（00:20:38）：所以美感是重要的，因为它能提升产品的实用性，增强产品的可访问性，而当这些因素相辅相成时，我们就能打造出更出色的产品。我认为单纯的美感，或者说单纯的工艺，没有实用性支撑，那就跟蓝光或路径一样。正确吗？这无法成就高质量的产品。所以关键在于将这些元素有机结合，朝着这个方向努力。（00:21:10）：但如果你真心希望你的产品、那些功能能够充分发挥价值，赢得用户的赞赏、尊重和重复使用，就要将其提升到更高的层次。要思考：“如何让用户使用起来感到愉悦？如何让产品像是为我量身打造，符合我的心理模型？” 这时候，工艺和细节执行的质量就至关重要了。

turns.zh: 哦，不错。好的。好吧。最后，质量是自豪感，美感是自豪感。如果我们能在工作中投入这样的用心，就会有更多人愿意与我们合作，因为他们希望看到自己付出的时间和对技艺的热爱得到认可和利用，并最终凝聚成真正有影响力的成果。我们把这视为重中之重，因为我们深知这对用户和合作伙伴都至关重要。美感是这一切的重要组成部分。

turns.zh: 是的，在如何将质量落地实践方面，我们确实有几件事可以探讨。因为人们往往容易陷入平庸的漩涡。想要突破到更高境界，真正创造出卓越体验，必然需要付出巨大努力，需要全员协同。我必须承认，我们仍在不断进步，尚未完全达成目标，追求卓越之路永无止境。（00:27:21）：我们打造网站的方式，是投入大量心血，确保呈现的内容能准确传达我们对用户的关怀。正因如此，我们格外重视这个过程，致力于将艺术与科学完美融合——既要兼顾创意，又要确保展示效果的技术水准。（00:27:49）：具体而言，我们通过设计、工程、产品合作伙伴和产品营销团队深度协作来实现这一目标。事实上，这是少数所有相关部门都汇报至同一部门的团队之一。因此，工程和设计团队在开发网站时，所有成员都向设计部门汇报。正如我们之前所说，如果团队成员同处一室，他们会紧密协作，持续交流想法。工程师会提出技术实现方案，设计师则会进一步优化创意。这种快速迭代的循环机制非常高效，尤其是在我们需要快速达成高标准要求时。

turns.speaker: Katie Dill
turns.en: But before I get into that, one of the things that has been driving a little bit of this process and the way that I've been thinking about how we can build better things at Stripe is actually I've been just talking to people, talking to different design leaders, product leaders, engineer leaders at different organizations and trying to understand how they go about it. There are a couple of themes that are clearly coming through. (00:29:28): Number one is that quality is definitely a group effort. You're sunk if you think that you can just hire some incredibly talented person and they'll do it, that'll be fine. The rest of us will do what we're doing and they'll do it, or that it's just one organization that's going to look out for quality or QA is going to solve it all for you. It really does need to be an organizational and a group effort. If you think about the way that you run the internal functions is going to show up in the outside and how clear you all are and how you're talking about it and the standards that you set inside and you're constantly reminding people of in the way that you communicate inside will then eventually show up outside. So, of course, keeping your talent bar high and then thinking about how those things really need to be cared for, that shared care across the organization is number one. (00:30:20): Number two is that there needs to be some amount of vision and alignment. So, if you hire all the best people in the world and you just set them out to go and do their thing, what are the chances that they're all going to end up with something that actually aligns pretty well? Even if they all have incredible taste and they're very good at what they do, there is subjectivity to every decision in some part. So, that they might end up with some things that are really great but don't fit together as a really nice whole. (00:30:49): The perfect example would be building a house. You have the person that works on the roof and the person that works on the deck and the person that does the siding, et cetera, et cetera, et cetera. A house is arguably far less complex than most of the technical products that we all know. Yet, there is painstaking effort put into having the plans and having a drawing of what the final thing is going to look like. There's a GC, there's an architect. And these people are helping to make sure that all those pieces fit together, and we should have that same care when we're trying to build products together. (00:31:19): I think a big pair on that is then the next piece, which is editing. And you might call that your GC or your architect or somebody that sees how all these things fit together, and then has an ability to help narrow and reduce and remove the things that don't fit. At Airbnb, Brian Chesky is the editor of all the things that come together. At the Economist, there's a chief editor. But other organizations, they might decentralize that approach, which is certainly possible, but challenging, because you do need somebody to help see these things come together. (00:31:53): That pairs with the next piece, which is about courage, the ability to actually say, "No, this isn't good enough." To have the resolve to just be like, "Almost, but no." Which is one of the hardest decisions I think leaders can make and certainly I've had to ever make in my career, too, is just a team puts all this care and effort into something and then you're going to say, "Actually, unfortunately we're just not there yet. Let's try again." That is, I think, incredibly important part of getting there and building the fitness of what you do. (00:32:28): Then, lastly, the thing that I've learned that will lead me to the example that you were asking about is that, in order to build quality, you really do need to understand it also from the user perspective, which gets me into my fixation with journeys, because that is how a user sees it. The user very, very, very rarely just deals with any aspect of what you build in isolation. There has to be a moment where they learn about it. There has to be a moment where they get to know it, and then there's a moment where they actually decide to use it, and then something just changed and now they need to use that product in some other way. You have to understand it from that point of view to really understand whether or not the quality is there. I think that's a critical piece of building teams that have empathy for their users. (00:33:16): So, we have been operationalizing that. All the things that I just mentioned, but one of the key pieces is to bring that approach to understanding the quality of the product. So, our goal was to set out to try to solve the fact that products can be shipped and they could be at their highest game when you ship them, they go through all the processes internally to be a high quality thing, and then it gets out into the world and then, over time, the quality regresses. Some of the reasons for that is that other things are being shipped. It's kind of like, again, back to an analogy of a house, imagine you have one room where you redo the molding and you paint the little aspects and you've put new plates on the lights, now all of a sudden that room is great, but it makes everything else look worse and the whole composite is worse. (00:34:10): That is something that can happen to products is actually they get worse over time. Then you organize a company oftentimes and parts to be able to focus on their key business areas. That's a very good thing because they get focused and they know what they're building towards and they get expertise and they're laser focused on that. So, ideally, they move faster. But what also happens is that they get so focused on that they forget about that piece of the journey, and how it all fits together, and not recognizing that part of their product experience is intimately tied to another. (00:34:44): So, what we did was we set out to, number one, increase the kind of awareness and accountability of leaders to own their journeys. What we have established are we started with 15 of our most important user journeys. 15 is somewhat of an arbitrary number. It's a number that we can kind of keep track of, but also has pretty good breadth, but is certainly not comprehensive of all the most important things. But 15 of our critical user journeys, the things that we know matter so deeply to our users, and we must get right at the highest level of quality possible. (00:35:20): Those 15 things then each have engineering, product and design leaders that are responsible for the quality of those products. They review these journeys, what we call walk the store, where they review them as if they're walking the floor of their store on a regular cadence, and they friction log what they experience, which I know David Singleton talked about on your podcast. They will write what they have seen, what's working, what's not working. They're viewing this from, they're trying to put themselves in the shoes of their user. This of course doesn't replace user research, but it substitutes it and it adds to that. (00:35:58): So, they go through the experience and noting what's working and what's not working. And very critically, it's a journey, so a lot of times it starts from internet search, it starts on Google trying to understand something, goes to the website, they end up on Docs, they end up in the dashboard, and they're seeing it as a user might. With that, they're able to find the entailments of the experience that may or may not be working. They jot that down, they file bugs, they reach out to the teams that may own the different parts of this experience, and then they score it. Then on, again, a regular cadence, we come together in almost like a calibration, where we meet and we talk about the score of their work. (00:36:40): It relates to performance reviews. Performance reviews, managers are assessing an individual's performance, which is hard. There's some subjectivity to it, just like understanding quality can be. But what we do as managers is we calibrate. We come together and we talk about, "Okay, how well is our interpretation of our ladders document? And how well does that performance align? And are we doing it consistently across the rest of the organization?" So, we do something very similar. We calibrate these scores because what we're really trying to do is not just the 15 essential journeys and the owners of those, we want to actually uplevel and bring more shared understanding of our quality bar across the company. These moments of calibration start that. Then having leaders do this creates this, number one, it cascades this idea of the importance of owning your journey and then also has upstream impact. (00:37:43): Because when people see the state of products in the wild as a user would, they learn a lot about what are some of the bigger opportunities that we can make to make the product better? What are some of the things that maybe we want to change in our process to make sure that we have even better things coming into the wild? One of the best parts of this is, since then we've learned that folks have seen that like, "Oh my goodness, our SEO for this particular product or the way we're articulating it doesn't align to actually how we want people to understand it later on in the journey. So if we improve this over here, we're going to improve outcomes later on." They're seeing that and they're now able to make that happen even faster to make some of the changes there. (00:38:27): Then my real favorite part is that we're hearing from folks that maybe at first didn't see this as necessary, that maybe in different functions that are just like, "Oh, I was so very focused on executing the technical ability of what I do on this thing, but I hadn't seen it from this lens before." Now there're actually converts of like, "Yes, this is a really important part of it." That goes back to the point of it's a group effort. You don't want just one function looking out for the quality of the product. So, having engineers and product managers and people of different disciplines walking the store, seeing the experience, feeling it firsthand, I think will lead to better care in all of the details that will aligned to better craft in the end.
turns.zh:
然而，在我深入探讨之前，有一个推动这一过程的关键因素，也是我思考如何在Stripe打造更优质产品的重要思路——那就是我一直在与不同组织的各级设计、产品和工程负责人交流，试图理解他们是如何开展工作的。通过这些对话，我总结出几个核心要点：  
（00:29:28）：首先，质量绝不是单个人的责任。如果你认为只要招聘一位天赋异禀的员工就能高枕无忧，其他人照常工作就行，或者认为质量管理只是某个部门或QA团队的专属事务，那就大错特错了。质量必须成为全组织共同的努力。你的内部运作方式会直接影响外部表现——团队对标准的清晰度、沟通方式以及持续强化规范的力度，都将最终体现在产品质量上。因此，保持高水准的招聘标准，并确保全组织对质量的共同关注至关重要。  
（00:30:20）：其次，必须要有清晰的愿景和协作机制。即便你招募了全球最优秀的人才，让他们各自发挥专长，但结果很可能难以形成整体协同效应。即使他们都具有卓越的审美和专业能力，每个决策也难免带有主观性。因此，最终成果可能很出色，但却无法完美融入整体架构。  
（00:30:49）：最典型的例子就是建房子。屋顶工、甲板工、外墙工等等，每个工种都各司其职。相比我们熟知的技术产品，建房子的复杂性要低得多。但即便如此，建房前仍会精心制定施工图纸，协调各方关系。Airbnb的布莱恩·切斯基就是产品集成的总协调员，《经济学人》则设有主编职位。其他组织可能将这项职责分散化，这固然可行，但挑战重重，因为始终需要有人统筹各方资源。  
（00:31:19）：与此相辅相成的是编辑角色。你可以把编辑视为总协调员或建筑师，负责统筹各方资源，剔除不符合标准的部分。在Airbnb，布莱恩·切斯基就是产品集成的编辑；在《经济学人》则设有主编职位。但其他组织可能倾向于分散管理，这固然可行，但挑战重重，因为始终需要有人统筹各方资源。  
（00:31:53）：这与下一个要点——勇气——紧密相连。勇气意味着敢于说“不行，这样还不够好”。要有决心说“还差一点，但不行”。我认为，这是领导者最难做出的决策之一，也是我在职业生涯中反复面对的挑战。当团队投入大量心血却未达预期时，必须勇于说“不行”，然后重新开始。这是我认为达成目标、打造优质产品的关键环节。
你们所做之事的实用性。（00:32:28）：最后，关于我所领悟的能让我解答你们所提问题的要点：要打造高质量的产品，确实需要从用户视角去理解。这也让我对用户旅程产生了执着，因为用户正是从这个角度看待产品的。用户极少会孤立地处理你所构建的任何单一方面。他们必须经历一个认知阶段，接着是熟悉阶段，然后是决定使用阶段，接着情况会发生变化，用户需要以新的方式使用产品。要从这个角度去理解，才能判断产品是否真正具备高质量。我认为这对打造对用户有同理心的团队至关重要。（00:33:16）：所以，我们一直在将这一理念付诸实践。刚才提到的所有要点，但其中关键的一点是，引入这种理解产品质量的方法。因此，我们的目标是解决产品上线后质量可能下滑的问题。产品上线时可能处于最佳状态，内部流程确保质量达标，但最终推向市场后却会出现质量退化。部分原因在于其他产品同时上线。这就像房屋装修的类比：你重新装修一个房间，粉刷小细节，换上新灯具，突然这个房间变得很棒，但却让其他房间显得更糟，整体体验下降。（00:34:10）：产品也会出现随时间质量下降的情况。企业通常会将部门组织成专注于核心业务领域的团队，这本质上是件好事——他们能专注目标、明确方向、积累专业知识、全力以赴。但理想情况下，这会提高效率。但同时也会出现问题：他们过于专注核心业务，忽视了整个用户旅程的衔接，未能意识到产品体验与其他模块的深度关联。（00:34:44）：所以我们的做法是：首先，提高领导层对用户旅程的认知和责任感。我们从15个最重要的用户旅程入手，这个数字是随意设定的——既便于管理又覆盖了关键场景，但远非面面俱到。选取这15个对用户至关重要的旅程，我们必须以最高标准确保其质量。（00:35:20）：每项任务都由工程、产品和设计负责人负责。团队定期开展“实地考察”式评审，记录体验中的摩擦点（大卫·辛格尔顿在播客中提及过）。他们会记录所见所感、优缺点，从用户视角审视产品。这并非替代用户研究，而是对其的补充和深化。（00:35:58）：他们亲身体验产品，记录每个细节。
关于工作成效与不足之处的反思。至关重要的是，这是一个持续改进的过程。通常，用户体验优化始于互联网搜索——用户在谷歌上查找信息，访问相关网站，最终进入文档页面或仪表板，以用户视角审视整个流程。通过这种方式，他们能发现体验中可能存在的痛点或改进空间。随后，他们记录这些问题，提交缺陷报告，与相关团队沟通，并进行评分评估。之后，我们会定期召开校准会议，共同探讨工作成效的得分情况。

这与绩效评估类似。绩效评估中，管理者需要评估员工表现，而这本身就充满主观性。但作为管理者，我们需要通过校准机制来统一标准。我们定期聚会，讨论以下问题：我们的评分标准与实际体验是否契合？各部门在执行过程中是否保持一致？通过这种校准机制，我们不仅关注15个关键用户路径及其负责人，更致力于在全公司范围内提升质量标准，达成共识。

这种校准机制的核心价值在于：通过让员工以用户视角审视产品现状，他们能更清晰地发现改进机会；通过反思流程优化，推动更高效的成果产出。例如，我们发现某产品SEO策略与用户体验不符，及时调整优化后，转化率显著提升。

最令人欣喜的是，许多原本对此不以为然的团队成员，如今已深信不疑。这种转变源于他们亲身实践：通过全流程参与，深刻理解用户体验全貌，进而推动创新落地。

turns.en: To your first point, 100%, they're all just forms of input. I'm definitely not saying do this instead of user research, do this instead of data. It's like these things in additional sense. Your users, they might not always say what's missing or what's wrong, or maybe they don't know that certain aspects of it could be better. We have, as I've mentioned, we are constantly looking at our processes and trying to figure out how we can make them better and better as an organization, as we've grown, things need to adjust. But also frequently enough that you're not missing that perhaps there's been a setback since. But, of course, my real hope is that they're happening weekly, just perhaps in different parts of the organization.
turns.zh: 关于你的第一个问题，我完全同意，这些都是获取反馈的不同方式。我绝不是说要用这个代替用户研究或数据，而是将它们作为补充手段。我确实认为亲自体验的强大之处在于，虽然我最支持用户研究，但即使听别人讲述体验也很有力，而亲身感受痛苦的感觉则更能让人直观地理解问题所在。比如，“哦，这个地方可以改进”。用户可能不会总是说出缺失或错误之处，或许他们自己也不知道某些方面可以做得更好。所以，在用户研究和直接听取用户反馈的基础上，再加上你的个人判断，这真的非常重要。（00:40:49）但你问到频率问题。正如我提到的，随着公司发展，我们不断审视流程，努力优化。我们现在每季度进行一次。每季度巡店并非唯一的时机，但这个时候我们会更新计分卡，并在仪表板上分享信息，让每个人都能看到。目前每季度一次的频率比较合适，因为这样有足够的时间做出实质性改进，你可以看到分数随时间变化。但也要足够频繁，以免错过可能出现的退步。不过，我真正的希望是能每周进行一次，哪怕是在组织的不同部门。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to ask a couple more questions so that folks can try this at home. I was just thinking this podcast is the opposite of don't try this at home. It's like, "Here, try this at home?"
turns.zh: 我想再问几个问题，让大家能在家尝试。我刚在想，这个播客和「不要在家尝试」正好相反。就好像在说：「来，回家试试吧？」

turns.speaker: Katie Dill
turns.en: Try it at home.
turns.zh: 在家试试吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. So, I want to try to give people a few more answers to questions when they're probably going to try to do this themselves. Who's in these meetings? Do you join these walkthroughs? Does David join? What do you suggest there?
turns.zh: 是啊。所以我想给那些可能自己尝试的人多提供些答案。这些会议都有谁参加？你会加入这些巡店活动吗？大卫也会参加吗？你有什么建议？

turns.speaker: Katie Dill
turns.en: Yeah. For what we're doing for each team is they do them themselves together. At bare minimum, it should be the engineer, product manager and designer doing it together. The reason why we like to see it happen together is, again, as we've talked about before, is that people bring a different perspective to something. Let's say somebody in the room might be like, "Oh my goodness, the load time didn't feel really good there." And like, "Oh, whoa, the way we're stating this is not consistent per page. And that's not on our design system." (00:42:41): So, it is really powerful to have folks come together and do it. In fact, David Singleton, who you mentioned, he and I do these things very regularly, too. This is outside the essential journeys program, but he and I walk the store and we'll just pick random flows and go through it together. I can't code, but he can. So, he'll do the code part and I'll be sitting there being, "What? Do they really do that? How can we make that better for them?" (00:43:08): I really love the multidisciplinary approach, but then when we do the calibration after the team has done these walkthroughs and they've gotten their own perspective and they fill out the scorecard based on our rubric for quality, we will come together in what we call PQR, product quality review. And they will take us through what they have experienced, and then they'll talk about, "So, this is why we've scored this, a yellow or a yellow green." Then we might have a conversation about that. (00:43:39): It's like, "Well, actually, that felt a little worse than you've described it. Actually, I think that we probably need to put more urgency on solving that." Or in some cases it's like, "Actually, that was pretty great. If you think about what we're trying to help somebody achieve at this moment that actually is really hitting the mark." (00:43:59): We will debate that there. In those meetings you'll have, yes, myself, David Singleton, Will Gaybrick, who leads product and business, and then various leaders from the organization that might be relevant to that area. We are trying to give people insight to what's happening across. Again, it's a multidisciplinary room. I'm trying to keep it not too large, because obviously it can be hard to have discussion, but it is very valuable to make sure, again, that we have the perspective of product marketing and the perspective of engineering, the expected product in the room as we discuss what our quality bar is.
turns.zh: 是的。我们让每个团队自己完成这项工作，最起码应该由工程师、产品经理和设计师共同完成。之所以希望他们一起完成，是因为正如我们之前讨论的，不同的人会带来不同的视角。比如，房间里有人可能会说：“天哪，加载时间太差了！”或者“等等，我们页面上的表述不一致啊。这可不是我们的设计体系该有的！”（00:42:41）所以，让大家一起完成这项工作真的很有帮助。事实上，你提到的David Singleton和我也经常这样做。这不在“基本旅程计划”的范畴内，但我和他会一起巡查商店，随机挑选一些用户流程，一起分析。我不会写代码，但他会。所以，他负责代码部分，而我会坐在那里问：“什么？他们真这么做了？我们怎么能让用户体验更好？”（00:43:08）我非常喜欢这种多学科协作的方式。但当团队完成这些走查后，他们会根据我们的质量评分标准填写评分表，然后我们会开一个叫做PQR（产品质量评审会）的会议。他们会向我们汇报他们的发现，比如：“所以我们给这个评了黄色或者黄绿色。”然后我们会一起讨论：“嗯，实际上，用户体验比你描述的更差。实际上我们可能需要更紧迫地解决这个问题。” 或者在某些情况下，他们会说：“实际上这做得很棒。如果你想想我们现在要帮助用户达成的目标，这真的很符合要求。”（00:43:59）我们会在会上进行讨论。参加会议的有我、David Singleton、负责产品和业务的Will Gaybrick，以及与该领域相关的组织内各级领导。我们试图让大家了解整个项目的进展情况。再说一次，这是一个多学科的团队。我尽量控制会议规模不大，因为显然讨论起来会比较困难，但确保产品营销和工程团队的视角都被纳入进来，这一点非常重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay. That makes a lot of sense. In terms of scoring, are you scoring individual steps of these journeys or is it yellow for segments? What are you scoring?
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的，我明白了。关于评分，你们是评分这些旅程的各个步骤，还是评分某些部分的黄色？你们具体在评分什么？

turns.speaker: Katie Dill
turns.en: The way the rubric works is so that, and we have a template for the friction log. So, people fill out a friction log and it'll be screenshots and then what they experienced. Then there is a tool to tag for each moment. It's like, "Oh, that was a nice touch." Or, "Ooh, that is not great. We should consider a fix." Or different levels of severity of like, "Oh my gosh, P0 bug, we need to fix this right now." So, they'll tag for different moments in the journey. (00:45:11): Then there is a summary score at the end, which is based on a rubric that we have that talks about the importance of quality from the point of view of usability, utility, desirability, and actually going to that next level of surprisingly great. Then we'll ask them to score on a whole what they felt of these things. Then that adds up to a summary score. Which we have also talked about the different ways of scoring. Is it a number-based system? Is it a letter-based system? Like A-minus and B?
turns.zh:
评分标准的运作方式是这样的：我们为摩擦日志准备了一个模板。用户需要填写摩擦日志，里面包含截图和他们的体验。然后，团队会用标签标注每个关键点。比如，“哦，这真是个贴心的设计！”或者“哎呀，这可不妙，我们得考虑改进措施。”再或者不同严重程度的反馈，比如“天哪，这可是P0级别的漏洞，必须立刻修复！” 用户会在整个产品体验过程中标注不同时刻的优缺点。

（00:45:11）最后，根据我们制定的评分标准得出总结分数。该标准从可用性、实用性、吸引力等维度评估产品质量，甚至更高层次的惊喜体验。用户需要对这些维度进行整体评分，最终汇总成总分。关于评分方式，我们也讨论过多种方案，比如数字评分系统、字母评分系统（如A-）等。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: [inaudible 00:45:42].

turns.speaker: Katie Dill
turns.en: Yeah. So far we have landed on a color system because, honestly, I think people can get a little tied around the axle on how you're measuring it, and to your point, especially in subjective things, and it's just like, "Oh, it's like, well, is it really a six or is it a seven?" We didn't want people to get a little too worried about how does... It's not meant to be an objective quantitative score. It is qualitative, it is judgment. We hire people for judgment, so we want them to bring that to the conversation. That's how we chose the score, because we felt that would actually lead to quicker but straightforward opinions and decisions.
turns.zh: 是的。到目前为止，我们选择了颜色评分系统，因为说实话，我觉得人们可能会被各种评分标准搞得头疼。比如用户会纠结：“这到底是6分还是7分呢？” 我们不想让大家太过纠结于具体的量化评分。这本质上是主观判断，我们招聘员工就是看重他们的判断能力，所以希望他们能在讨论中发挥这一优势。这就是我们选择颜色评分的原因，因为我们认为这样能更快地形成清晰的意见和决策。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: At a lot of companies, you have these reviews and the founders share all this like, "Oh, this is broken, this is busted." And as a product team, you're like, "Goddammit, we have these goals we got to hit. We have this roadmap. And now we're going to get a hundred things that the founder's like, 'Got to fix this.'" I'm curious just how you tell teams to take this stuff and prioritize it amongst all the other things they're going to do. Is it just up to them, is they're like, "Need to fix this"? Anything you can share there, but just how to actually operationalize taking this feedback and doing something with it?
turns.zh: 很多公司在做产品评估时，创始人会大发雷霆：“这破了，这糟透了！” 作为产品团队，我们会忍不住抱怨：“该死，我们还有目标要达成，有路线图要执行，现在创始人又要我们改一堆东西！” 我很好奇，你们是如何让团队在众多任务中优先处理这些反馈的？是完全交给团队自己决定吗？还是让他们主动说“必须修复这个问题”？能否分享一些具体的操作方法？

turns.speaker: Katie Dill
turns.en: Yes. Yeah. I've seen some organizations talk about when they're doing planning, you do your OKRs quarterly or half year or year, whatever, recommendations of like, 10% of your time should be spent on fixing things, and 20% on growing things, and the rest on keeping the lights on, whatever it might be. Yes, I've seen different companies build a recommendation based on certain percentages of how they think teams should be spending their time. (00:47:28): We at Stripe think that, first and foremost, is that we have to make sure that folks are, number one, hired with the fact that they have great judgment and care for what they build, and they take pride in it. That's number one. Then, you can give a lot of trust to people based on that commitment to building great things that they will use that in their decision-making. Then, of course, it needs to be very clearly advocated for at the highest levels of the...
turns.zh: 是的。我见过一些公司在制定OKR时，建议团队每年或半年进行一次回顾，其中10%的精力用于修复问题，20%用于增长，其余时间维持现有运营。是的，我见过很多公司根据特定比例为团队分配时间，但在Stripe，我们认为首要任务是确保团队成员在招聘时就具备良好的判断力，关心自己打造的产品，并为此感到自豪。这才是最重要的。然后，基于这种打造优质产品的承诺，我们可以给予团队充分的信任，让他们在决策中充分发挥这种判断力。当然，最高层还需要大力倡导这种理念。

turns.speaker: Katie Dill
turns.en: ... Advocated for at the highest levels of the company. And with that, I think that fuels people's thinking as they're building their plans, but there is iteration in the plans and we do have multidisciplinary people making the plans together. So it's like, "Oh, okay, are we advancing these features? Are we going to be building growth? And is that improving the quality as well?" And so I think that's how we together get to it, but there's no formula that we ask people to.
turns.zh: ……在公司最高层得到了大力倡导。我认为这为人们制定计划提供了思路，但计划过程中会不断迭代，我们确实有跨学科团队共同制定这些计划。比如，他们会问：“我们是否要推进这些功能？我们是否要着力于增长？这样做能否提升质量？”通过这种方式，我们共同达成目标，但并没有一个固定的公式要求人们必须遵循。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So basically what I'm hearing is it's the cultural just people are hired with this expectation we are going to focus on quality and we'll prioritize things even though they may not move metrics because we know that this will generally improve and grow the business.
turns.zh: 所以我理解的是，这种文化意味着人们入职时就带着这样的期望——我们将专注于质量，并优先考虑相关事项，即便这些举措短期内无法提升指标，但我们深知这最终会推动业务发展。

turns.speaker: Katie Dill
turns.en: Part of it though is showing how it moves metrics, because I think that is a dangerous belief that is absolutely out there, as we talked about earlier, but that actual quality improvements do increase growth, they do improve the bottom line. For example, we saw that folks were reaching out to support because they didn't know the state of how one of their invoices was performing. And when we dig in, we realized it's, well, we had a button that looked nice, but it wasn't super clear, and so they didn't know how to access the thing that they were trying to do. And so by improving that, we decrease the need for them to have to reach out, which is clearly not their want to have to call somebody to find the answer to their problem. And so with that, we've made an improvement and we, of course, improve the bottom line because of that. (00:49:38): So I actually think that maybe one of the steps that somebody should consider in their organization is just you have those examples, every company does, where quality leads to better business outcomes and to talk about those and make them known, because I think it's actually a false belief that it's one or the other, it's like, "Are we going to work on quality and it doesn't move the metrics? And where we do." Some of them are longer term and so you have to look out for a while to see that change and the beliefs of your customers or how often they're sharing your product or how often they're succeeding in what they're trying to do, but some of them are short-term impacts and that is an important thing for people to be aware of because it will give them ideas of, oh, we could do this in our team too, we could have a higher quality product and actually move the business metrics.
turns.zh:
但关键在于要证明质量提升如何能转化为实际增长。我之前提到过，这是一个危险的误区。但实际上，质量改进确实能促进增长，提升利润。比如，我们发现用户因为不了解某张发票的状态而向客服求助。深入分析后发现，我们虽然设计了一个美观的按钮，但操作指引不够清晰，导致用户无法完成操作。通过优化这一点，我们减少了用户的求助需求，毕竟没人愿意打电话才能解决问题。这就是改进后的成果，自然也提升了利润。
（00:49:38）：所以我认为，在组织中可以考虑的一个步骤就是分享那些成功案例——每个公司都有这样的例子，质量提升带来了更好的业务成果。要多多宣传这些案例，让大家意识到，质量和增长并非非此即彼的关系。比如，有些改进需要长期积累才能显现效果，比如客户对产品的认可度或使用频率；而有些则能短期见效，这对团队非常重要，能激发他们的灵感：哦，我们的团队也能做到！我们也能打造高质量的产品，进而推动业务增长。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything you do in how you evaluate performance of teams that helps prioritize this sort of thing? So generally it's just, cool, this team moved this metric by a ton, they're doing great. Is there anything that you bake into performance evaluations at Stripe, especially for product teams that help them understand and prioritize some of these things that may not obviously move metrics other than just broadly we believe great experiences are going to improve growth?
turns.zh: 在评估团队绩效时，是否有方法能优先考虑这类因素？通常来说，我们会关注团队在某个指标上取得巨大进步，认为他们表现出色。Stripe在绩效评估中是否有特定指标，特别是针对产品团队的，能帮助他们理解并优先处理那些短期内可能无法显著提升指标，但从长远看对业务有益的改进？

turns.speaker: Katie Dill
turns.en: Well, I think one part is being clear on what impact means, because I do think that in some companies impact is just, okay, what business metric did I move and how much? And there are certainly really important impact projects that folks can have that maybe they're multi-quarter, multi-year, and so maybe you didn't move this incredibly important business metric in one quarter, but actually the work that you are doing is instrumental to the success of the business. So there's that. And then, like you said, there are perhaps quality efforts that are harder to measure or they're longer term, but they're still impactful. So I think number one is that when you're thinking about how to come up with the rubric for how you're going to judge performance, it's just really honing in on what does impact mean, and then a lot comes from that and being able to and celebrate and recognize great work happening even when it's not necessarily materially moving that number. (00:51:59): The other part of it is we have a ladder system. So it's a document that's not meant to lay out here's the checklist of all the things you need to do, but it's a guide for this is what is expected in your role and at this level, and in these documents we talk about the importance of things like quality in that what we pursue is building these things that are great. And another part of that is also the operating principles, which is the thing that we align on underneath all of these levels and ladders systems that we have. And our operating principles include meticulous craft. It is one of the things that is really important to us as an organization is just having that meticulous care for all that you do, whether it's you're designing the space that we work within or that you're creating the API or that you're building the interface or that you're talking to people on support calls, the meticulous craft is something that is actually expected of everybody.
turns.zh:
嗯，我认为首先要明确“影响力”具体指什么意思，因为我确实发现有些公司对影响力的理解仅仅停留在“我移动了哪个业务指标，幅度有多大？”这样的层面。当然，确实存在一些真正重要的影响力项目，这些项目可能需要数个季度或数年的时间才能见效。或许你某个季度没有显著提升某个关键业务指标，但实际上你所做的工作对业务成功至关重要。所以这就是第一层含义。正如你所说，可能有些质量改进工作更难衡量，或者需要更长时间才能显现效果，但它们同样具有重大意义。因此，我认为在制定绩效评估标准时，首先要明确“影响力”的定义，其次要确保即便某项工作未能直接提升关键指标，我们也要能够认可和表彰其背后的卓越贡献。

（00:51:59）另一个关键点是我们采用了晋升体系。这份文件并非详列所有任务清单，而是为各级员工设定预期标准的指南。在文件中，我们强调质量的重要性，追求打造卓越产品。同时，我们还制定了运营原则，作为各级晋升体系的核心准则。其中“精益求精”至关重要——无论是设计办公空间、开发API、构建界面，还是处理客服电话，每个环节都必须精益求精。这是我们整个组织所秉持的核心价值观。

（00:54:09）：接下来我想转向另一个话题，也是我最后想重点探讨的领域——团队建设与领导力。你曾在三家高速增长的公司担任设计主管，其中Airbnb和Stripe两家都是全球顶尖公司，且以卓越设计闻名。我想问一个宽泛的问题：在组建、领导和管理大型团队方面，你有哪些心得？当我抛出这个宽泛问题时，你能想到什么？

turns.speaker: Katie Dill
turns.en: One of the things that has stuck with me through all the trials and tribulations of leading, and as I've already laid out for you in the very beginning of this call, haven't always got it right, but one of the things that has been a clarifying force as I think about growing and leading teams, it's actually something I learned at Airbnb when we were there together, it's a formula sort of. So performance equals potential minus interference.
turns.zh: 在领导团队的种种考验中，有一点始终伴随着我。正如我在通话伊始提到的，我并非每次都做得完美，但在思考团队成长与领导力时，有一个启示性的理念源自我在Airbnb的经历，那就是一个公式：绩效=潜力-干扰。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that.
turns.zh: 我很赞同这个观点。

turns.speaker: Katie Dill
turns.en: And I really like this, it's pretty simple, but it's a good reminder that, as a leader, one of the things that you are of course driving towards is trying to get better performance so that your team feels more purpose and motivation and is excited about their work and that you're building greater things for your customers and you're having more business effect, and, of course, performance. But the key pieces of that, of course, is potential, so thinking about how you increase potential, which would be, of course, hiring really well, developing the talent and helping them grow and increase their own potential to do better and greater things. And then paired to that though of course is decreasing the interferences, which could be that lead weight on top of great talent, because you can hire the best people in the world, but like a muscle atrophying underneath a cast, if there are interferences that are holding them back from doing great work, they're going to burn out, they're not going to enjoy the work, they're not going to be as successful, and you will not get as strong of performance from it. (00:56:14): And so I really do think of this constantly as to how can I increase potential, how can I decrease interferences? And over time, especially as your company grows, you're going to have to keep doing that. The design work is never done in designing a team, because the more people you bring in, the more it puts your processes in a faulty state. I have intentionally run teams where you get to a point where it's like running hot, it's just like, "Okay, we've outgrown our processes." And that's okay because then you can learn as to, okay, this is how people are actually trying to work and this is how we actually can improve it. So making those changes as needed helps to make them more sought after and more informed in terms of as you improve the processes. (00:57:05): One of the things that I've been working on since I worked back at Airbnb was this idea of improving awareness of the things that are happening. What happens at a lot of companies, especially as they grow, is people lose touch with what's happening in different parts of the organization, and everybody's got a doc, their PRD, where they've written down what they've done and it's got tons of words that nobody really understands and keywords for the different projects, and that isn't the best way to lead to clarity. And I'm a strong believer that a picture tells a thousand words and a prototype saves a thousand meetings. What we do, and I've been doing it for the last decade or more, is having people within the design team share as a screenshot or a prototype of what they're working on in a shared deck. (00:57:54): And so they add this to a slide, in Google Slides decks every couple of weeks, and we get to see what's happening across the design team. And this is really important for all the designers because they could see, whether or not they're a team of 10 or 170 or whatever it might be, what is happening, and they can say, "Oh my gosh, you're working on that surface, so am I. And let's talk about it. Or Oh, that's an interesting pattern, maybe we could use this in more places." And we send it to the product managers and the engineer leaders and the leaders in the company because it is also a really great way for them to understand what's happening and what are we building together. Because going earlier, as I talked about, the importance of thinking about things as a journey, so what's happening in the marketing side, what's happening in this aspect of the product and seeing how all these pieces really fit together, that has been absolutely one of the things I will take wherever I go, whatever I do, because it has just been a very, very useful tool.
turns.zh:
嗯，我真的很喜欢这个观点。这听起来挺简单的，但它很好地提醒了我们，作为领导者，我们当然要致力于提升团队表现，让成员感受到使命感和动力，激发他们对工作的热情，为客户创造更大的价值，并最终获得更显著的业务成果。但其核心要素无疑是挖掘潜力——如何提升团队成员的潜力。这就需要招聘优秀人才、培养人才、帮助他们成长，进而提升自身能力，以达成更高的目标。与此同时，还要减少各种阻碍因素，比如那些压制优秀人才的沉重负担。即便你能招到世界上最顶尖的人才，但如果存在阻碍他们发挥潜力的因素，他们也会精疲力竭、失去工作热情，难以取得成功，最终也无法创造出色的业绩。  

（00:56:14）所以我一直在思考如何提升潜力、减少阻碍因素。随着公司规模的扩大，必须持续关注这两个方面。团队设计工作永远没有终点，因为引入新成员会让现有流程失效。我曾故意组建过一些团队，当它们发展到某个阶段时，就会进入“高负荷运转”模式。这时我们就会意识到，“好吧，我们的流程已经跟不上节奏了。” 这没关系，因为这时候我们就能了解团队的真实运作方式，并据此改进流程。  

（00:57:05）自从回到Airbnb后，我一直在致力于提升团队对动态信息的感知能力。很多公司在发展过程中，员工会逐渐与组织其他部门脱节。大家虽然有PRD文档，但里面堆满了无人能懂的术语和项目关键词，这远非高效沟通之道。相反，我坚信一张图片胜过千言万语，一个原型胜过无数次会议。过去十年来，我一直让设计团队成员每隔几周就在Google Slides中分享他们的设计截图或原型。  

（00:57:54）这些信息会被添加到幻灯片中，让所有设计师都能实时了解团队动态。这种方式对团队至关重要，无论是10人团队还是170人团队，每个人都能清晰掌握进展。他们会感叹：“天啊，你也在做那个界面，我也是，让我们聊聊吧。” 或者惊呼：“这个设计模式很有意思，或许我们可以多用在其他地方。” 我们还会把这些成果分享给产品经理、工程师负责人和公司高管，因为这也是他们了解全局、协同推进的重要方式。正如我之前提到的，要把工作视为一个旅程，各个部门的协同至关重要。
看到所有这些拼图碎片是如何完美拼合在一起的，这绝对是我无论去到哪里，无论做什么都会铭记于心的一件事。因为它实在是一个极其实用、无比宝贵的工具。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I remember that at Airbnb, and there's nothing more fun than just looking through a bunch of awesome designs and products that are in motion and in a deck form is so handy, just flip through what's going on around the company, I'm like, "Oh wow, look at this thing. That's amazing." And it's interesting that ends up in a deck, it feels like Figma would be really good for that too, but somehow decks are still really handy for simple things like that.
turns.zh: 我记得在Airbnb，浏览一堆超棒的设计和动态产品真是太有趣了。以Deck形式呈现的演示文稿特别方便，随手翻阅公司动态时，我总会惊呼：“哇，看看这个，太棒了！”有趣的是，这种演示文稿形式在Figma中也能实现，但Deck格式对于简单展示还是非常实用。

turns.speaker: Katie Dill
turns.en: One of the key pieces is just keeping it really low maintenance. Yes, the design team would definitely prefer that it would be in Figma, but critically I want all functions to be able to look at it. And if not everybody is on Figma, if they were, that would be great too, but if they're not, it's just flipping through really easy, touch of a button, you can just send it off, it's behaviors that people are really used to and commenting. But maybe one day Figma.
turns.zh: 关键在于保持其易用性。没错，设计团队肯定更希望用Figma，但关键是让所有人都能查看这些内容。如果不是所有人都用Figma，用的话当然更好，但即便没有Figma，快速翻阅也很方便——只需点击按钮就能发送，这正是人们熟悉的操作模式，还能随时评论。不过说不定哪天Figma就能实现这些功能了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And the way you do that is it's just like a scheduled call for all designers, add your stuff to this deck and then you email it out every two weeks I think you said?
turns.zh: 具体做法是定期组织设计师会议，把成果添加到Deck中，然后每两周发送邮件分享成果，对吧？

turns.speaker: Katie Dill
turns.en: Yeah, and we experiment with how often we ask folks to share and also the granularity of what they're doing. It is not meant to be a status check. We're not asking everyone, "Show us what you're doing." It's more of what are the projects that are happening? And we might ask, "Show us the medium and large projects," if there's such, it's too much going on and all of a sudden it's a 200-page deck and no one's going to flip through it. So we have experimented and evolved that depending on the team size, and I think right now we're at monthly sharing of it, and that seems to be working pretty well. It used to be biweekly, which I loved because I really love looking through, but if it's feels like it's a arduous task then it's not succeeding.
turns.zh: 是的，我们也在探索分享频率和内容粒度。这个活动不是为了检查进度，也不是让每个人都汇报工作，而是展示正在进行的项目。可能我们会要求分享中大型项目，因为如果内容太多，最后会变成200页的Deck，没人愿意翻看。所以我们根据团队规模调整了分享频率，目前定为每月一次，效果不错。之前是每两周一次，我个人更喜欢频繁分享，但如果让大家觉得负担过重，就没意义了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And especially knowing designers, they'd want to make sure it's the best version of what they've done, and it takes all this extra time to, okay, we got to make this beautiful mock to show [inaudible 01:00:39] working on.
turns.zh: 尤其是设计师，他们总想确保展示的是自己最出色的成果，这就需要额外花时间制作精美的模型来展示[01:19:29]的进展。

turns.speaker: Katie Dill
turns.en: And actually another part of it that is another benefit of opening up the curtain a little bit of certainly we have to take things seriously in terms of confidential work, it's work in progress, it's not ready to go live, we're not ready to critique all the details about this. We do need to make it very clear to folks that this is work in progress, but also that it is really beneficial to bring the work out because what isn't great is that you get to the end of the project and people have worked tirelessly on it for some long stretch of time and then find out that, oh my gosh, this is the same project that we're doing over here and this can be completely redundant, or these two things are on a path to collide. (01:01:25): So we want to know that sooner because it, absolutely, in the end of the day, will make the work better, save time. And so opening up that curtain and showing the work in progress, it can feel hard at first, but I think people have started to see the benefits in doing that and then usually that will lead to better outcomes in the long run in the culture too.
turns.zh: 另一个好处是适度开放视野。当然，我们必须严肃对待机密工作，确保未完成的项目不被泄露。我们要明确告知大家这是正在进行的工作，尚未准备好上线，不必深究每个细节。但让大家看到进展还是很有好处的，因为项目结束时，人们往往发现与其他团队重复工作，或者两个项目方向相冲突。（01:16:25）所以早点发现问题，最终能提升工作质量，节省时间。开放视野、展示进展一开始可能让人不适应，但我相信大家会逐渐认识到其价值，长期来看也会提升团队文化。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Going back to this formula you shared, which I love, performance equals potential minus interference, is there an example that comes to mind of helping with the interference where you found that, oh, wow, this is really slowing things down and you change something?
turns.zh: 回到你分享的这个公式——我很喜欢它，绩效等于潜力减去干扰因素。能否举个例子，说明在处理干扰因素时，你发现某些做法确实拖慢了进程，于是进行了调整？

turns.speaker: Katie Dill
turns.en: It actually goes back to org design that we talked about earlier and where people sit. So when I joined Lyft, as I mentioned to you earlier, I was like, oh, I had learned from the experience that I had at Airbnb and I came in needing to transform the organization, and was hopefully much better at it because I had learned so much. What actually was going on there is that the way that the team was organized before I got there was that actually physically the design team sat separately. They sat in a room that was just beautifully designed, separated from engineering and product and all the other functions by a locked door. And that was really interesting to see because of course there were a lot of benefits to it, which is that design had this very safe space for creative discovery and exploration and communication, there was work all over the walls, it was wall to wall whiteboards, and it was just absolutely a place where creativity could thrive.
turns.zh: 这其实要追溯到我们之前讨论的组织设计，以及人员的职位安排。正如我之前跟你提到的，我加入Lyft时，本以为能凭借在Airbnb积累的经验来推动组织变革，但实际上却困难重重。问题在于我加入前的设计团队是分隔开来的，他们位于一间精心设计的会议室里，与工程、产品等部门隔着加锁的门。这种物理分隔看似有诸多好处——设计团队能在安全的环境中进行创意探索和沟通，墙上贴满了草稿纸，白板随处可见，确实是个激发创造力的理想场所。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It sounds exactly like the Airbnb situation, by the way.
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，这听起来和Airbnb的情况如出一辙。

turns.speaker: Katie Dill
turns.en: The current Airbnb situation or the past?
turns.zh: 是现在Airbnb的情况，还是过去的情况？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The original, the [inaudible 01:03:05] times.
turns.zh: 是Airbnb最初的组织架构时期。

turns.speaker: Katie Dill
turns.en: Yeah. And absolutely there are a lot of tie-ins to what I had seen. And the interesting part about how actually teams were working is that you would see that there was a lot of wasted work and there was a lot of misalignment in what we were trying to do because there was product managers and engineers that were sitting alongside each other making decisions and talking about the work and deciding things, and then designers were sitting over here in this other room and they were working on something, and then they'd meet up and it's like, "That's not aligned. No, that doesn't fit the goal. And you went that way, we were supposed to go over this way." And so interference in the sense that it was wasted work, it wasn't actually aligned to the goals, it was slower. And there were definitely benefits, there was real reasons for doing this, and I know there are companies including Apple that have separation of these things. (01:03:58): But I think if you're going into that way of working, there's probably a lot of other decisions you need to make too in terms of the way the teams work. And so what I was seeing there was just the composite of all these aspects coming together that was not leading to more efficient and less interference. And so what we did was to evolve the way we were working and bring better alignment to the different functions. (01:04:22): And, again, had done it with an approach about listening and came into that with a better understanding of getting to know the team and getting to know engineering and product and see what our goals were together so that when we were making changes we were making the changes together and we actually were aligned so that on the day that we opened the doors and brought design and product together and had spaces for folks to work together and they actually sat with each other, we still kept the creative space for this is where we'll do grits, this is where we'll do working sessions, this is where the folks that don't work in an embedded fashion we'll sit, but we had the best of both worlds in that way. And so with that alignment of the way that the teams were working together, there was much faster iteration cycles, better clarity on how the work was working, and we still kept and protected that room for creative space, literally the room in terms of figuratively speaking for allowing for creative exploration, but more aligned.
turns.zh:
是的。确实有很多地方和我之前的经历相呼应。有趣的是，团队实际的工作方式存在诸多问题：比如，产品经理和工程师们会坐在一起做决策、讨论工作、拍板定案，而设计师们则在另一个房间里埋头工作，结果经常出现沟通不畅、目标偏离的情况。比如，“这不符合我们的目标”、“你应该那样做，而不是这样做”。这种沟通不畅导致工作效率低下，目标执行不力。

当然，分工协作也有其合理性，比如苹果公司就将产品与工程分开管理。但我认为若要采用这种模式，团队协作方式需要全面调整。当时我所观察到的，是各个职能部门之间严重脱节，缺乏有效协作。

（01:03:58）：但我认为如果要采用这种工作方式，团队协作方式还需要进行更多调整。比如，我们通过倾听需求，更深入地了解团队和工程、产品部门，共同明确目标。这样一来，当我们将设计和产品团队整合，提供协作空间时，设计师和工程师们就能坐在一起交流。我们还保留了创意空间——既有实体区域，也为非全职设计师提供了工作场所。通过这种方式，我们实现了团队协作的无缝衔接，迭代周期大大缩短，工作效率显著提升。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And just so I understand, essentially you reorged the teams and not just physically moved people, but you changed the way the product and design and eng team was even organized?
turns.zh: 那我理解的是，你们不仅是重新安排了团队的位置，还调整了产品、设计和工程团队的组织架构？

turns.speaker: Katie Dill
turns.en: Yes, literally and figuratively we broke down the wall and brought the teams physically together so that they would work together, and then we had an org chart where it's like, okay, these designers are working on driver, these designers are working on rider, these designers are working on the safety team, and then they would sit with their respective engineers and product managers. And then as I talked about earlier, we would come together at key moments to make sure that we as a design function, we're still aligning on shared goals about the overall experience, but also making sure that we could work well with our partners.
turns.zh: 是的，从字面上和隐喻意义上来说，我们打破了部门壁垒，让团队成员实体地聚集在一起协作。比如，设计师们会分组负责司机端、乘客端、安全团队等模块，与各自的工程师和产品经理紧密合作。正如我之前提到的，在关键节点我们会召开会议，确保设计团队围绕整体用户体验的共同目标保持一致，同时确保与合作伙伴的有效协作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So interesting that that was a recurring pattern at the places you went. I imagine Stripe was not like that, there was not all designers sitting in that locked room.
turns.zh: 有趣的是，你去过的那些公司似乎都存在类似的模式。我猜Stripe应该不是这样的，他们的设计师应该不会被关在密室里。

turns.speaker: Katie Dill
turns.en: Not in a locked room. When I joined Stripe, it was a Zoom universe, so it's a little bit different, but even today we have a studio space where we have all the great tools of craft, and when you do go into the offices, we do have places where designers sit together, especially in the functions that aren't embedded. For example, we have brand and marketing creative, we have the website team, and we have folks that work across all of the things that we do. And so for sure there usually is some sort of creative space, which I actually think having a physical space for creative discovery and exploration and having that up on the wall, I love that so much. And I go into the office about halftime now, and I think over time we'll probably build that out more and more, because it is really powerful in addition to having teams sit by the disciplines that they work with every day.
turns.zh: 并非在封闭的房间里办公。当我加入Stripe时，公司仍处于远程办公阶段，所以情况有所不同。但即便在今天，我们仍设有工作室空间，配备了各类创意工具。进入办公室后，设计师们会集中在特定区域，尤其是那些不受部门限制的团队。比如，我们有品牌与营销创意团队、网站团队，以及负责各类业务的同事。因此，通常都会有专门的创意空间。我特别喜欢这种能让创意灵感自由碰撞的物理空间——将作品展示在墙上，这感觉太棒了。如今我每周只需半天时间到办公室办公，相信未来这种空间会逐渐完善，因为除了让团队成员与日常合作伙伴紧密协作外，它还能激发创作灵感。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It reminds me of a quote I have on my wall that I think I found in the Rick Rubin book, but it's by someone else, so I don't know exactly where I found it, but it's the object isn't to make art, it's to be in that wonderful state which makes art inevitable.
turns.zh: 这让我想起墙上挂的一句话，似乎出自里克·鲁宾的书，但具体出处记不清了。原句是：“艺术的目的不在于创作艺术，而在于进入那种让艺术自然产生的美妙境界。”

turns.speaker: Katie Dill
turns.en: Ooh, that's good. I like that very much.
turns.zh: 哦，这真有道理。我特别喜欢这句话。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: By Robert Henry. That's what I try to do in this little podcast studio that we got here.

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything else that you think would be useful to share either from scaling design teams or broadly?
turns.zh: 在扩展设计团队或从更宏观角度出发，你觉得还有哪些经验值得分享？

turns.speaker: Katie Dill
turns.en: I think one of the other tendencies I see of companies in different stages of their growth is a fear of bold ideas. What happens is that... It can happen at small sizes and then it can happen at large sizes actually, it's just that a fear of shaking things up too much or big ideas with lots of things changing at once are really hard to measure. And so actually if we just make an incremental approach, it's very measured and we know what the outcome is going to be, it feels safer, I can get it done in the quarter, and depending on how your performance is managed, that might be more attractive. And so that is a dangerous tendency, because I think if we go back to what quality means, and you think about it as, well, quality is really your users are the judge of that, and the way that they experience things oftentimes across products, across surface, across time, if you just think about these incremental approaches to the scope of whatever that is that you own, you are very likely not to make the whole thing better. (01:08:57): So I think we have to fight against that. And the way I look at it is, the way I talk about it is reach for the stars and land on the moon. And what I mean by that is that vision work is really important, and I think sometimes you can get a bad name because you can end up with some folks that are doing vision work that goes nowhere, and they make a beautiful deck and then it gets seated on a shelf and nobody ever builds it. That is not what I'm talking about here, that is not what I recommend, but actually vision work that absolutely does look at the entirety of the experience, a comprehensive approach, a journey approach, and thinks about how these various things may come together to be better, and sketch out the ideal version. And I think Brian Chesky talks about it, I think it was the 11-star experience I think he once said.
turns.zh:
我认为，在企业成长不同阶段，我所观察到的另一个趋势是，对大胆创新的恐惧。具体来说，当公司规模较小时，人们往往会回避冒险；而当公司规模较大时，人们又会担忧改革引发的剧烈震荡或一系列变革措施的不可控性。因此，人们往往倾向于采取渐进式改进策略——这种方法可控性强，结果也容易预见，短期内就能达成目标，而绩效考核机制也会让这种策略更具吸引力。但这种谨小慎微的做法其实很危险，因为归根结底，质量的定义应该由用户来评判——用户在不同产品、不同界面、不同时间段的使用体验才是最重要的衡量标准。如果只对现有业务范围进行渐进式改进，很难真正提升整体体验。

（01:08:57）所以我们必须克服这种倾向。在我看来，解决之道在于“志存高远，脚踏实地”。这意味着愿景规划至关重要，但有时人们会因为愿景工作徒劳无功而留下负面印象——他们可能只制作了一份精美的PPT，却最终束之高阁，从未付诸实践。这并非我所倡导的愿景工作，而是要全面审视整个用户体验，采用综合性方法，构想各要素如何协同优化，并勾勒出理想状态。布莱恩·切斯基（Brian Chesky）曾谈到过这一点，我记得他曾提到“11星级体验”。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: [inaudible 01:09:45] stuff. That's what we talked about a couple of times in this podcast.
turns.zh: [01:09:45]这些内容我们在播客中多次讨论过。

turns.speaker: Katie Dill
turns.en: Exactly. Looking at it as a journey. It's not the five-star approach, it's not the six-star approach, but the 11-star approach, but show what that ideal version is, because if you don't know what that is, what are the chances that you're going to increment yourself to the right outcome in the end? And as I talked about before, building the house, you want to see what that picture looks like and how all these pieces come together, and I strongly recommend you want to see what it looks like in an ideal form, because you can always work back from that. (01:10:17): And so it's like, "Okay, if this is what we want to get to, this is what our product is going to look like in two years, how do we get there?" And what very likely is it's a team effort and various parts of your organization are going to have to own various parts, and maybe we ship this piece first so that we can study it and learn and make sure that the data is good before we move to the next piece, I'm not suggesting you have to ship the whole thing at once, but that North Star lays out the process in a way that I think allows for big risk taking in a way that is measured and thoughtful and actually also feels like progress as you step towards that versus trying to get their day one and likely end up giving up.
turns.zh:
没错。将其视为一个旅程。这不是五星级方案，也不是六星级方案，而是11星级方案，要勾勒出理想版本。因为如果连理想版本都未清晰界定，又怎么能指望通过渐进式改进最终达成目标呢？正如我之前所说，建造房屋时，人们需要先看到整体蓝图，了解各个构件如何拼合在一起。我强烈建议先构想理想状态，因为这样才能倒推回现实路径。

（01:10:17）具体来说，比如：“好，如果这就是我们要达成的目标，未来两年我们的产品会是什么样子？我们该如何实现它？” 很可能这需要团队协作，组织内不同部门需各司其职。或许我们先推出某个模块，进行测试、收集数据再推进下一步。我不是说要一次性完成整个项目，但北极星方法论能以可控、深思熟虑的方式规划大胆尝试，让人们在迈向目标的过程中感受到进展，而非徒劳地追求完美首秀，最终却半途而废。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that, reach for the stars, land on the moon. That could be a metaphor for so many things. Let me try to squeeze in one more tactical tip for people listening. If someone's hiring a designer, so someone that's not a designer, just a founder of product team, what should you look for that may be a red flag or something that you want to look for to feel good that they're going to be a good fit?
turns.zh: 我喜欢那句话——“触及星辰，登上月球”。这句话可以隐喻很多事物。让我再给听众们分享一个实用的招聘建议。如果有人要招聘设计师——比如产品团队的创始人而非专业设计师——应该留意哪些可能的警示信号，或者哪些方面能让你确信对方会是合适的人选？

turns.speaker: Katie Dill
turns.en: The key, I think, to keep in mind is it's easier to teach tools and process than it is taste and character, so I would certainly pay a lot of attention to that. Their hit rate for great judgment and great taste, and how they've honed that, even if they're not very experienced, just to see do they have that natural inclination for great things. The other piece of it is that certainly you want to find somebody with great talent, for sure, and high craft, but you...
turns.zh: 我认为关键在于，相较于工具和流程，品味与性格更难培养。因此，我会特别关注这一点。即便他们经验不足，也要考察他们是否具备出色的判断力和敏锐的审美眼光，以及如何不断磨练这些能力——这能反映出他们是否天生就对卓越事物有追求。

turns.speaker: Katie Dill
turns.en: Talent, for sure, and high craft, but you also want to find somebody that's humble. Folks that are really good at what they do aren't always, but humility is a really important part. I think it's a really important part for anybody on a team because if you're working on a team, you need to work together. And it is important that they have that respect and empathy and understanding and enthusiasm for the folks around them, but also the users. Humility means that they're going to pay more attention to what the users are saying and hopefully be curious about what's working and what's not, and strive to navigate these things to make it better. The last piece would just be hustle or chutzpah. I'm not sure exactly what's the right way to put it, but the design and the creative functions is the act of creation. (01:12:53): And it's scary. To take a blank piece of paper and propose something that you think is better, is scary. To have the courage to say, "This is not good enough and we should do it again," is scary. Having somebody that has that courage inside them to fight for great is pretty important. And that hustle to try to execute on that rapidly is, of course, essential as you're hiring at any stage company. (01:13:23): Lastly, I think you were asking in particular, especially with younger companies or with startups, I think one thing that can be hard, it's like do you hire a more junior doer or a more senior thinker/operator? It's like if you had all the money in the world, all of it. But I do think in your early stages you probably do need a doer, but it is important to also have that lens of how do you build an organization that's user-focused and the way that they operate and the way that they work together, and bringing a strategy that will help to be user-focused from the start. Maybe a great way of doing that is having a more senior leader, design advisor, and then a kind of executor or doer full-time on the team.
turns.zh: 当然，人才和精湛技艺至关重要，但你还需要找到谦逊的人才。真正优秀的人未必总是谦逊，但谦逊是关键品质。对团队成员和用户怀有尊重、同理心、理解力和热情至关重要。谦逊意味着他们会更关注用户需求，保持好奇心去探究哪些方法有效、哪些无效，并努力改进。最后是进取精神或勇气。我不太确定该如何准确表达，但设计和创意工作本质上是创造行为。（01:12:53）：面对空白的纸张，提出自己认为更好的方案令人心生恐惧。敢于说“这还不够好，我们应该重新来过”同样需要勇气。拥有这种为卓越而奋斗的勇气至关重要。当然，在招聘任何阶段的公司员工时，快速执行的能力也必不可少。（01:13:23）：最后，你特别提到，尤其是在初创公司或年轻企业中，可能面临的难题是——是招聘初级执行者，还是更资深的战略思考者/运营者？假设你拥有无穷无尽的资金，但在初期阶段，你可能确实需要执行者，但同时也要构建以用户为中心的组织架构，关注团队的运作方式和协作机制，并引入从一开始就以用户为导向的战略。或许最有效的方法是聘请一位资深设计顾问，并在团队中配备全职的执行者或执行者。

turns.zh: 我们稍微谈到了不同学科的重要性，以及质量是团队共同努力的成果。我希望这不会冒犯到我的职能，但说真的，设计的核心本质上就是意图。你需要在思考设计对象时，有意识地做出决策：比如设计一个门把手时，要考虑它是否能传达出“我是要推、拉还是转动？手感是否舒适？生产是否容易？安装和拆卸是否便捷？”这些都是可以做出的有意识决策，无论你是设计师、工程师、产品经理还是其他职能，都能注入这种意图。（01:20:17）：当你思考谁会受到影响，谁会使用这个设计时，可能范围非常广泛——从设计门把手到设计组织架构，再到制定战略。显然，优秀的设计还需要创造力，以及对美的敏锐品味。正因如此，拥有这些创造力和审美能力的设计专才，无疑是组织中极其宝贵的财富。第一天，每个人就能带来更多用心和意图，我相信这最终会带来更好的内部和外部成果。（01:20:56）：我认为你们的播客就是卓越工艺和高品质的典范。前几天我刚和我丈夫说起这事儿，提到做这个播客时。我就想，你们这些播客……每分钟传递的实用知识比大多数内容都要多。我不知道这是不是你们衡量的一个指标，但我很欣赏你们不让嘉宾讲述个人背景的做法。因为嘉宾讲背景固然有趣，但那不是真正有用的信息。关键在于，“我可以把这些信息拿去运用，带到自己的团队，让工作更出色。”你们显然深思熟虑过这个决策。嗯，我不知道你们是否就是因此做出这样的选择。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Absolutely. That is exactly [inaudible 01:21:40]

turns.speaker: Katie Dill
turns.en: Okay, great. I also love the way that you set these things up. You had said to me, in the thing that you set me, it's just like, "If it's not good, we're not going to ship it." And you set it in very nice ways, by the way. But at first I had this like, "Oh gosh, what if it's not good?" But I also had this moment of like, "Well, that's pretty great because if it's not good, he's not going to embarrass me to the rest of the world, hopefully." And I love that because that was that courage that I was talking about earlier, too, of that you're not going to let bad go out, because you know that each one of these little things will end up leading to a belief of the level of quality of what somebody can rely on getting when they listen to your podcast. Again, one workout isn't going to be a six-pack, but every one of those things will end up leading to better quality overall. I don't know, kudos to you. You're nailing it. So great.
turns.zh: 好的，太棒了。我也喜欢你们设定这些规则的方式。你之前给我看的文件里写着，“如果不够好，我们就不会上线。”你们的表述方式很棒。不过一开始我会想：“天哪，要是做得不够好怎么办？” 但随后我又想：“嗯，这其实挺好的，因为如果做得不好，希望他至少不会让全世界都看笑话。” 我很欣赏这一点，因为这也正是我之前提到的勇气——你不会让劣质内容流出，因为你知道这些小细节最终会影响听众对播客质量的信任。再说一次，一次锻炼不会练出六块腹肌，但每一次努力都会提升整体质量。真心为你们点赞。你们做得很棒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Katie, what a nice way to end it. I really appreciate that. That's exactly how I think about it, actually. You cracked my whole strategy of just making it as concretely useful as possible. I was actually on David Perell's podcast recently and he had this really good way of describing this, which is exactly what I've tried to do, but I haven't put my words into it of make it as useful as possible per minute without removing the humanity. And I realized that's what I do, is I could cut all the stories of everyone's backgrounds, but that sucks. It's optimize for value and concrete, tactical advice, but also make it fun and human and interesting. (01:23:15): So thank you for the kind words. And with that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. I've got a number of questions for you. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 凯蒂，这样结束真是太棒了。我真的很感激你这么说。这正是我对此的看法。事实上，你完全颠覆了我“尽可能让内容实用”的策略。我最近参加了大卫·佩雷尔的播客，他对此有很好的阐述，这正是我一直努力做到的，但我还没有用文字准确表达出来——如何在不削弱人性化因素的前提下，每分钟都提供尽可能多的实用建议。我意识到这就是我的做法——我本可以省略所有人的背景故事，但那样就太糟糕了。要优化价值和具体的行动建议，同时还要让内容有趣、有人情味。（01:23:15）：所以谢谢你的赞美。接下来是我们激动人心的闪电问答环节。我有几个问题要问你。你准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Katie Dill
turns.en: I'm ready.
turns.zh: 我准备好了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, let's do it. What are two or three books that you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 好的，开始吧。你向别人推荐得最多的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Katie Dill
turns.en: One, How to Win Friends and Influence People. It's an oldie but a goodie. I forget how many years old it is, but many, many decades. I think it was in the 1930s? The cover is funny. You might be embarrassed to read it on a bus, I don't know. But the learnings from it are timeless, and I've actually read it four times and I can always do for another because it is a great reminder of just how important the way you articulate things are. And not in a negative or gross kind of way, but people care first and foremost about themselves. That's the body that they're within, that is the context that they're within. Recognizing that can be really powerful as you think about leading teams, as you think about working with other people, as you think about being a good spouse, whatever it might be. I'm a big fan of that one. (01:24:19): The other one is a newer book, I think actually still a couple of years old. It's about the Wright Brothers by David McCullough, I think. I've been learning how to fly, and so I'm very obsessed with this, but I think it's a book that's relevant to everybody. Especially even entrepreneurs, because it just talks about the impossible challenge of nobody thought it could be done. Even the American Institute of Science didn't think it could be done. And these individuals that had the resolve and the commitment to make it happen. I think also the power of this beautiful partnership. Of course, they're brothers. That doesn't always mean you get along, but they're brothers and they did, and it's a beautiful story. Big, big, big fan of that. (01:25:05): And then third book, I would just say is... Actually, I brought it over because I knew you were going to ask me this question. I don't know if you could read that, but The Boy, the Mole, the Fox, and the Horse. This book was given to me by Jenny Yarden, which I think you may know. It's wonderful. It's a beautiful story. It makes you laugh, it teaches you a thing or two, and one of the best quotes in it is, "One of our greatest freedoms is how we react to things."
turns.zh: 第一本是《如何赢得朋友并影响他人》。这是一本经典之作，虽然年代久远，但依然金玉其外。我忘了它出版多少年了，但至少有几十年了吧？我想是1930年代？书皮很有趣。可能你在公交车上读它会觉得尴尬，但书中的道理永不过时。我已经读了四遍，还能继续读下去，因为它能很好地提醒你，如何清晰地表达想法有多重要。不是以消极或粗俗的方式，而是人们首先关注自己。这是他们身处的身体，也是他们身处的环境。当你考虑领导团队、与他人合作、成为好伴侣时，认识到这一点会非常有力。这一本我很喜欢。（01:24:19）：第二本是新出的书，应该还有几年吧，是大卫·麦卡洛写的关于莱特兄弟的。我最近在学飞行，所以对这本书很着迷，但我觉得它对每个人都有启发。特别是创业者，因为它讲的是一个看似不可能完成的挑战——连美国科学院都认为做不到。但这些人有决心和承诺，最终成功了。还有这段美好合作的力量。当然，他们是兄弟。这并不意味着他们总是相处融洽，但他们是兄弟，而且成功了，是个美好的故事。我对这本书爱不释手。（01:25:05）：第三本书，我带来了，因为知道你会问这个问题。不知道你能不能读到，《男孩、鼹鼠、狐狸和马》。这本书是珍妮·亚登送给我的，我相信你也认识她。很棒。是个美丽的故事。能让你开怀大笑，还能学到东西。里面最棒的一句话是：“我们最大的自由之一，就是如何应对事物。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Very Buddhist.
turns.zh: 很有佛系哲学意味。

turns.speaker: Katie Dill
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: What is a recent favorite movie or TV show that you really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 最近你最喜欢的电影或电视剧是什么？

turns.en: Oppenheimer was amazing. And TV show? Shrinking. And that one was really good, and it actually really surprised me how funny and positive it was, because the trailer for it does not give that impression. But it was really good.
turns.zh: 奥本海默太棒了。那部电视剧呢？《收缩》（Shrinking）。那部剧真的很棒，它的幽默和积极态度让我非常惊喜，因为预告片给人的印象完全不同。不过那部剧确实很棒。

turns.zh: 告诉我你最引以为傲的作品。之所以这么问，是因为这能帮助我了解他们的品味和判断力，了解他们的动机，以及他们认为什么是优秀的作品和成功的结果。还能让我稍微了解他们的兴趣所在和关注点。

turns.zh: 太棒了。Toniebox。我应该也带过来的。它就像个软软的盒子，但其实是个音箱。孩子们可以控制它。控制方式是通过小人偶。比如《美女与野兽》里的贝儿，或者《冰雪奇缘》里的艾莎，把小人偶放在顶部，就能播放故事或歌曲。你还能录下自己的声音，讲故事给孩子听。他们自己就能操作，甚至掉到地上也没关系。不过Toniebox确实很棒。

I'll communicate better expectations tomorrow." And it's like those joke signs that "Free beer tomorrow." Because very easily, tomorrow just always moves on. And I needed to remind myself that it's actually, it is now today. Tomorrow is now today.
turns.zh: 我虽然不常说出口，但我的珠宝盒里一直贴着便利贴，经常看到。明天就是今天了。我的意思是，经常我在脑子里想：“明天再做吧。明天再吃得健康点。明天再考虑那个愿景。明天再更好地沟通预期。”就像那些玩笑标语“明天免费啤酒”。因为明天总是轻易就过去了。我需要提醒自己，现在就是今天。明天就是今天。

turns.en: Is there a lesson that your mom or dad taught you that has really stuck with you, especially as a newish parent?
turns.zh: 有没有你父母教给你的、至今仍铭记于心的道理？尤其是作为新手父母后。

turns.speaker: Katie Dill
turns.en: I think about this a lot. I am a mom of twin girls, and I feel so lucky that my parents raised me to see that accomplishment is based on merit and hard work. They never made me feel like because I was small and that I was not as strong as somebody, whatever it might be, that I wasn't able. My dad had me chopping wood and mixing cement as a young kid, and that certainly led me in one part to be a designer, but also to be able to pursue leadership. Even though sometimes I'm comfortable willing to be in the room where I am vastly outnumbered by people that don't look like me or just not letting that hold me back. (01:29:31): And actually, I thought about that the other day because I was riding in a Lyft to the airport. This was also at 4:00 AM, so it was a really hard time to be in a Lyft to gone to the airport. The driver was telling me about his kids, and actually he had twins. It was one boy and one girl, and so we were talking about twins. He's like, "Yeah, yeah, yeah, my girl, she's my princess. My son doesn't understand why I don't let her take out the garbage and why her job is to sweep and that's his job." He's like, "I'm not going to let her take out the garbage." I was sitting in the back of the car wondering, "Should I tell him, you're screwing it up?" (01:30:07): Just because she's a female doesn't mean that she's not able to do the jobs, even the hard ones and even the bad ones taking off the trash. I really do think that I'm so fortunate that that was never the way that my parents were looking at it. Now, today, I feel like that is very much a part of a little bit of my chutzpah and willingness to step out there because I hadn't been held back from those hard jobs earlier.
turns.zh:
我经常思考这个问题。作为一对双胞胎女儿的母亲，我深感幸运——我的父母从不让我觉得成就源于特权或捷径。他们从不因为我个子小、力气不如别人而贬低我。他们让我从小就参与体力劳动，比如砍柴、搅拌水泥，这些经历不仅让我成为设计师，更赋予我追求领导力的勇气。即便有时我会因身处全是非本族人的环境而感到不自在，但我从不让这些阻碍自己。

（01:29:31）前几天坐Lyft去机场时，我又想起这件事。当时是凌晨四点，打车去机场的难度可想而知。司机聊起自己的孩子，原来他也有对双胞胎——一男一女。我们聊起双胞胎时，他说：“是啊，是啊，我女儿就是我的小公主。我儿子不明白为什么不让他倒垃圾，扫地是女儿的活儿。”他强调：“我绝不让女儿倒垃圾。”我坐在后排，想：“我该不该提醒他，这教育方式有问题？”

（01:30:07）仅仅因为性别不同，就认为女孩做不了重活，甚至倒垃圾这种“脏活累活”，这太荒谬了。我很庆幸父母从不这样看问题。如今，这种思维模式让我拥有了大无畏的精神，敢于挑战难题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Final question. You mentioned that you fly planes, and this is actually related to my last question. I guess one that I was going to ask if that's true, you mentioned it is true. Is there a lesson that you've taken from learning to fly and flying that you've brought into product, leadership, design? Anything come to mind?
turns.zh: 最后一个问题。你提到自己会开飞机，这和我的上一个问题有关。我本想问这是不是真的，你确认这是事实。请问从学习飞行和飞行经历中，你获得了哪些能应用于产品、领导力或设计的启发？有没有什么特别的感悟？

turns.speaker: Katie Dill
turns.en: First of all, learning to fly has been such an amazing experience because there haven't been many things in my adult life where you feel like yourself going from knowing nothing about something and being able to do something, and what an incredible journey that is. Whether it's learning a language or whatever, that is awesome and highly recommended. But one of the key things that has definitely sat with me from the experience of learning how to fly that I definitely thought about how to bring it into my work is that when I was getting to the stage of being able to do things myself... My instructor is sitting there next to me and usually is right there at the controls with me, so if something goes wrong when I'm flying, he's right there. (01:31:46): I remember one of the first times when I was learning how to land where he moved his seat back. A lot. And so he was now out of touch with the controls. He could jump there if he needed to, but he really pulled back. And it was such an incredible visceral experience. I was like, "He trusts me. Right now, he is showing his faith in me to take this and take this challenge on." And I think about that all the time. It's just like, "How can I show my team, people I work with, my support and trust in them to take that challenge on?" I can't always move my seat back, but what might be the way? And so that's been a pretty great example of something I want to pull forward.
turns.zh: 首先，学习飞行是一段令人惊叹的经历，因为在我的成年生活中，很少有事情能让你从对某事一无所知到能够独立操作，而这段旅程实在令人难以置信。无论是学习一门语言还是其他任何技能，这都是很棒的，而且我强烈推荐。但学习飞行这段经历中，有一点让我印象深刻，我至今仍在思考如何将其应用到工作中——当我逐渐能够独立操作时……我的飞行教练通常会坐在我旁边，紧盯着控制台，这样万一我飞行时遇到问题，他就能及时介入。（01:31:46）我记得我刚开始学习降落时的第一次经历，他把座椅往后调了很远，这样他就与控制台失去了联系。虽然他可以随时介入，但他故意把座椅调得离得很远。这是一种令人震撼的直观体验。我当时想：“他信任我。现在，他是在向我传递信心，让我迎接这个挑战。”我时常回想这件事。如何向我的团队、同事传递这种信任，让他们也勇敢地迎接挑战呢？虽然我无法把座椅调得离得那么远，但或许有其他方法。这就是我想要借鉴的一个绝佳例子。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is an awesome metaphor. I feel like this whole episode is just full of beautiful metaphors. Also, just full of beauty. Katie, thank you so much for being here. Two final questions. Where can folks find online if they want to reach out and maybe ask some questions? And how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 这真是一个绝妙的比喻。我觉得整期节目都充满了美妙的比喻，也处处洋溢着美好。凯蒂，非常感谢你今天的到来。最后两个问题。如果听众想联系你或者提问，可以去哪里找你？听众如何能为你提供帮助？

turns.en: First off, please do find me online because, as I talked about, we are in the pursuit of trying to build excellent things and it's always a work in progress, and so I'm always interested to learn how others do it and see how we can improve our own methods. I am Lil_Dill on Twitter, and then I think that name was taken on Threads, so I'm Lil_Dilly, with a Y, on Threads, and then I'm on LinkedIn and find me there. We're hiring, so definitely reach out at our job board, too. Stripe.com/jobs. Definitely check us out. We definitely would love to hear from you.
turns.zh: 首先，请一定在网上关注我。正如我之前提到的，我们一直在努力打造优秀的产品，而这始终是一个持续改进的过程。因此，我很乐意了解其他人是如何做事的，并借鉴我们的经验。我在Twitter上的账号是Lil_Dill，在Threads上用的是Lil_Dilly（加个Y），在LinkedIn上也可以找到我。我们正在招聘，所以也欢迎在我们的招聘页面申请职位：Stripe.com/jobs。期待你的加入。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Katie. Again, thank you so much for being here.
turns.zh: 凯蒂，再次感谢你的到来。

turns.speaker: Katie Dill
